opening: Day two in the spire.
Writing this on my knee by lantern light.
Note for the next one up: read this and save yourself some trouble.
If anybody finds this, the stew is in the left pack.
Third floor of the day. My legs have opinions.
Short note, the pencil's nearly gone.
Quick note while the guards are busy being somewhere else.
To whoever comes up after me: hello, and mind the step.
The mayor said to write everything down, so here's everything.
Rest stop. Bread, water, a bit of a sit.
Still alive, still hungry, still going up.
Nobody in town will believe this, so it's going on paper.
Halfway through the day, by the feel of my boots.
My spouse made me promise to write. So: writing.
Another floor, another note.
First time up here. Not the last, I hope.
Morning, if it's morning. Hard to tell in here.
The kids asked for a full report. Here it is.
Sitting on a chest I'm not allowed to open yet.
The baker bet me two loaves I wouldn't write anything. Pay up.
Here's what this floor had for us today.
Stopped to catch my breath and my thoughts.
Not much light to write by, but here goes.
Expedition log, if a few scribbles count as a log.
Back home they're having supper about now. Up here:

roots: Found a crystal that hums when you sing at it. Sang it the market song. It hummed back, slightly off-key, just like the market.
A stone sentry stood in the doorway for ages before it moved. Polite, really. Then it swung.
The roots of this place grow through the walls like an old tree through a fence. Some of them are warm.
Tapped a wall and the whole cave rang for a minute. Won't do that again; something big woke up.
Picked up a shard of the Core. It ticks in my pocket like a pocket watch that's lost count.
There's moss down here soft enough to sleep on. Did not sleep on it. Thought about it a lot.
The steps here are worn in the middle, like a church step. Somebody walked up and down these for years.
Hanging roots everywhere, tickling the back of your neck. Spent the whole floor swatting things that weren't there.
Saw a little crystal growing out of a crack, no bigger than a thumb. Left it alone; it's got enough to deal with.
The sentries fall apart into light when you beat them. It's a lot nicer than it sounds.
Took the long way round a sentry with a shield. Took the very long way round, to be safe.
The air down here smells like rain on stone, the first minute of rain, before everything gets wet.
archive: Bridges made of bookshelves. You walk along the spines of books over nothing at all. Don't look down. Do read the titles.
A paper moth landed on my sleeve and refiled my handkerchief. I want it back.
Found a book of recipes from some old town. Copied out one for plum jam. Less sugar than you'd think.
The card drawers sigh when you open them. Opened one just to hear it again.
A shelf full of letters, all tied with string. Didn't read them. Well. Read one. It was about goats.
Got caught in a shower of pages thrown by something with book wings. Paper cuts in places I won't name.
The ladders run on rails all by themselves. Rode one three times on purpose.
Every lamp in the reading room is dark, but they look like they're waiting for someone to sit down.
Found a book with my town's name on the spine. Empty inside. Waiting, maybe.
There's a brass pipe as thick as a barrel running up through the shelves, and it smells of old ink.
The moths put back every book you take. Took the same book four times to see if they'd get annoyed. They did.
An entire wall of maps. Couldn't find our town on any of them. Felt left out, then proud, somehow.
workshop: Hammers bang away on anvils with nothing on them. All that work and nobody to pay. Felt right at home.
A clockwork hound chased me, then fetched my hat back. We don't know where we stand with each other.
Everything here is copper gone green at the edges, like coins left in the rain.
Found a drawer of screws, all facing the same way. Somebody here cared very much.
The belts run from wheel to wheel and the whole floor hums like a beehive with a job to do.
Burned my thumb on a pipe. It's still a nice pipe.
Saw a forge breathing with nobody working it. Warmed my hands. Said thank you. It didn't answer.
There's a conveyor belt that carries nothing round and round for ever. Rode it twice. It was nice.
A hound brought me a gear the size of a dinner plate and seemed very proud. Took it, to be polite.
Got lost among the chimneys. Followed the smell of oil out. Works every time.
Found a tool I don't know the name of. Brought it for the smith; he'll pretend he knows.
The guards here wind up before they lunge. You can hear it coming. Fair play to them.
gardens: Cherry trees under a glass roof, petals falling and never quite landing. Caught one for my daughter.
The canals are so clear you can count the pebbles. Counted forty, then a vine tried to tie my laces.
Found a pear tree trained flat against a wall like a candlestick. Our farmer would cry.
The guards here prune. Got pruned. My hat's shorter now.
Ate a strawberry from a bed here. Don't tell the gardeners, they're very strict.
There's a bench with a heart carved into it and somebody's initials. Sat there a while. Nice bench.
The water here smells of blossom. Washed my face in it and smelled like a wedding for an hour.
Stepped on a seedling by accident. Three vines came at me at once. Fair enough.
Brought back a cutting in my hat. The farmer says it's either an apricot or trouble.
Bees as big as my fist, all very busy, none of them interested in me. Insulting, really.
A whole terrace of flowers I've never seen, every colour, and one smell for all of them.
Saw the light come through the glass roof onto the water and forgot to be careful for a whole minute.
galleries: Water everywhere, warm, lit from below. Put a hand in and heard somebody humming a lullaby. Took the hand out quick.
A ray made of glass and fog came up out of a pool and knocked me in. Drier now. Not by much.
There's a fish tank as big as a barn with a pike in it that looks at you like you owe it money.
The aqueducts go on arches higher than the church roof. Walked along the top. Won't again.
Found a fountain still running after who knows how long. Drank from it. Tasted of summer.
Watched the bubbles to see where the big thing would surface. Worked. Wrote it down for the next one.
Slipped on a wet stone and slid three yards on my back. Very graceful, nobody saw.
The pools are in steps, one spilling into the next, like a staircase made of water.
Got my boots soaked to the ankle. Squelched through the whole floor. Squelching now.
Saw a fish with whiskers longer than the mayor's. Didn't tell the mayor.
Every sound echoes three times here. Coughed once, the hall coughed back twice.
The light in the water moves like it's thinking about something.
ice: Ice pillars, snow ceiling, and up above the lights of the north pouring across the sky. Stood and stared till my nose froze.
A snow giant hit me on the arm and the arm went slow for a minute. Hit it back slowly.
Breath comes out in clouds up here. Made a few shapes. One looked like a goat.
The frost on the walls makes patterns like handwriting. Couldn't read it. Tried.
Slid down a frozen ramp on my backside. Faster than walking, worse for dignity.
Cracked an ice pillar and it fell on a guard. Not proud. A little proud.
Found an old sledge frozen into the floor with a lemon crate on it. Lemons, up here. Empty, sadly.
Wore every layer I brought. Looked like a haystack. Was a warm haystack.
The cold here doesn't bite, it just leans on you. Kept moving so it'd lean on someone else.
Icicles as long as a ladder hanging over the doorway. Went through on tiptoe.
The lights in the sky turn green, then pink, then green again. Nobody back home will believe the pink.
Everything creaks. Ice, snow, my knees.
spores: Brought home a glowing mushroom. Not allowed in the house. It lives in the shed and lights the chickens.
Mushrooms tall as the chapel, glowing purple underneath. Walked under them like under umbrellas in the rain.
Stood in a cloud of glowing dust and almost lay down for a nap. Bit my tongue and kept walking.
The moss is so deep my boots disappeared. Found them again. One of them.
A puffball on legs burst in my face and I sneezed glitter for an hour.
Spores float upwards here, like snow that changed its mind.
Picked a little mushroom for the kids. It's glowing in my pocket. The pocket's glowing. I'm glowing a bit.
The forest breathes out, slow and soft. Breathed with it for a while. Felt better.
Saw a mushroom shaped like a lady in a big hat. Bowed to it, just in case.
Took a nap. Didn't mean to. Dreamed of supper. Woke up hungry and with moss in my ear.
Everything smells of damp bread in here. Not bad. Not good. Interesting.
Kept a spore in a jar. It's asleep. Looks peaceful. Envious.
hive: Honeycomb walls taller than houses, every cell glowing. The whole floor hums. My teeth hum too.
Stuck my finger in a cell to see if it was honey. It was. Licked it. No regrets.
Got chased by a swarm. Ran. The swarm was faster. Hid behind a flower. The flower helped.
There's a word inside some of the cells, glowing in the wax. One said 'tomorrow'. Nice word.
Saw a round, slow guard patching up the others like a nurse. Went for it first. Felt mean. Worked.
Everything's sticky. My hands, my boots, my notes. This note is sticky. Sorry.
Climbed flower terraces all day. Smelled like a jam shop. Hungry the whole time.
Brought home a bit of wax for candles. Smells of summer when you light it.
Watched the bees moving between the terraces, all working together, nobody shouting. Unlike our building site.
The hum changes when you sing. Sang. It sang back. Not a bad duet.
Got stung once. Swelled up like a loaf. Still worth it for the honey.
A big bee with a crown landed near me, looked me over, and left. Felt judged. Fairly.
observatory: Telescopes everywhere, and all of them pointing at the floor. Looked through one. Saw something shining deep underground.
Amethyst grows out of the walls here in purple clusters. Knocked off a little one for my sister.
The ceiling is painted with silver stars. Lay on my back and counted till I lost count.
A falling star cast a shadow on the floor first. Moved out of the shadow. Good advice, that.
Brass rings turn overhead by themselves, slow as a sleepy clock.
Found a star chart with lines on it that look like roads. Copied a bit. Might be nothing.
Got lost among the telescopes. Followed the coldest draught to the door.
It's so quiet here you can hear the rings creaking a floor away.
Sat at a desk covered in maps and pretended to be very clever for a minute.
Looked through a telescope at the ground and saw a river and a ford with good stone. No idea where it is. Lovely, though.
The purple light makes everyone look a bit ill. Including me. Especially me.
Wrote my name in the dust on a brass plate, then wiped it off. Felt wrong to leave it.
summit: Decks of white stone and nothing over the rail but cloud. Didn't look down. Looked down. Regretted it.
Lanterns in a big ring, all dark, each one taller than a person. Patted one. Felt silly. Patted it again.
The wind up here tried to take my hat twice and my notebook once. Tied everything to everything.
Could see the whole world from the top. Rivers like threads. Couldn't see our town, but felt it was there.
The guards up here are every kind at once. Remembered everything from the floors below and used it all.
The floor moved under me. Not shaking — moving, like a deck on a boat. Held on to the rail and swore politely.
Saw a gold light at the far end of a hall and went toward it without deciding to.
The air is thin and cold and smells of nothing at all. Breathed slowly to make it last.
Ate my last bread on the highest deck of the world. Best bread I've ever had.
It's so bright up here that shadows look blue.
There's a lantern with our town's mark on it. Touched it. It was warm. Didn't tell anyone. Telling you.
Found a bench right at the top facing the sunrise. Somebody put it there on purpose. Good on them.

feeling: Not bad for a first trip.
Tired, but the good kind.
My feet hurt. My heart doesn't.
Can't wait to tell everyone, and nobody will believe half of it.
Worth every step.
Miss the soup at home, though.
Glad nobody saw my face just then.
Going up again tomorrow, if my knees allow.
It's beautiful in here, I'll give it that.
Honestly, I laughed more than I was scared.
Somebody built all this. Wish I could shake their hand.
Felt very small and very lucky at the same time.
Lost a glove, found a story. Fair trade.
The pay had better be good.
Think I'm getting the hang of this.
My pack is heavier and my head is lighter.
Kept thinking of the kids the whole way.
Said a quiet thank you to nobody in particular.
Every floor is stranger than the last, and I like it.
Hungry again. Always hungry in here.
Not scared. Well. A little. Not much.
Would bring the whole town if it were safer.
Feels like the place is watching, but kindly.
Didn't want to leave. Did anyway. Supper's waiting.
Will be telling this one at the tavern for years.
signature: — %s (yes, the one from the bakery queue)

place: This layer remembers a fishing town on a grey northern sea.
This layer remembers a hill town where every street was a staircase.
This layer remembers a river town built half on stilts.
This layer remembers a town of red roofs in a valley of orchards.
This layer remembers a crossroads town that was mostly inns.
This layer remembers a quarry town cut into the side of a white cliff.
This layer remembers a small town on an island with one bridge to the shore.
This layer remembers a desert town around a single deep well.
This layer remembers a forest town whose houses were built around living trees.
This layer remembers a mountain town where the snow came up to the windows every winter.
This layer remembers a marsh town of boardwalks and lanterns on poles.
This layer remembers a town of potters, with kilns smoking on every corner.
This layer remembers a town on a lake so still the whole town lived twice, once upside down.
This layer remembers a windy town of mills on a long green ridge.
This layer remembers a town that grew up around a ford with good grey stone.
This layer remembers a terraced town on a slope of vineyards.
This layer remembers a town of weavers where coloured cloth hung across every street.
This layer remembers a harbour town where the ships were bigger than the houses.
This layer remembers a town in a canyon, where the sun reached the streets only at noon.
This layer remembers a meadow town that had a fair every week and a quarrel after every fair.
This layer remembers a town of beekeepers on a hillside covered in heather.
This layer remembers a border town with a wall older than anyone could explain.
find: On a table lies a ledger of mended nets, every line in a different hand.
A child's chalk drawing still covers the doorstep: a spire, a lot of yellow.
In a cupboard there is a jar labelled 'Do not open until the wedding'.
A letter is half written on the desk, the pen still beside it, the ink still wet in memory.
The bell rope in the square has been knotted and re-knotted by a hundred hands.
On the wall of the tavern someone has kept a tally of who won at cards, for forty years.
There is a recipe for honey cakes pinned by the oven, with three different people's corrections.
A pair of small boots stands by the door, just outgrown.
In the chapel, a hymn book is open at a song nobody in our town knows.
There is a map of the town with every house labelled by who lives there and what they're best at.
A loom stands mid-pattern, a blue thread waiting in the shuttle.
On the mayor's desk there is a list headed 'Things to fix', and every line is crossed out.
A garden plot is marked out with string, the seeds in a paper twist beside it, not yet sown.
The doors have no locks, only latches, every one worn shiny.
There is a board by the well with notices: lost goat, found goat, goat returned with apologies.
In a workshop, a half-built cradle waits on the bench.
A kite hangs tangled in the church tower, and nobody has tried to get it down.
A rack of fishing rods by the bridge, each one carved with a name.
The baker's shelf is full of loaves, still warm in the memory of this place.
On a bench by the square someone has carved, 'We were happy here. Don't forget the steps are slippery.'
There is a letter tube in the square with a message still rolled inside, addressed to 'whoever's next'.
On every windowsill there is a pot of the same small yellow flower.
who: Whoever lived here argued about the weather in letters to three other towns.
The people here built slowly and mended everything twice.
The townsfolk here sang while they worked, badly and all at once.
Whoever lived here kept their doors open in summer and their kettles on in winter.
The people here traded with five towns of the network and owed each of them a pie.
Somebody here wrote down every birthday in town and never once missed one.
The people here were famous across the network for terrible jokes and excellent bread.
Whoever lived here grew more than they needed and gave the rest away.
The people here were very proud of their wall and polished the gate every spring.
The townsfolk here had an argument about where to put the bakery that lasted eleven years.
The people here sent their light south every winter and asked only for songs back.
Whoever lived here named every cat in town and wrote the names on the wall.
The people here built a tavern before they built a town hall, and never regretted it.
The townsfolk here walked a day to help a neighbouring village raise a roof, every year.
The people here held a lantern night every spring and danced until the lamps ran out.
Whoever lived here believed a house should face the sunrise and a bench should face the view.
The people here were quarrelsome, generous and early to bed.
The townsfolk here measured twice, and then a third time, out of respect.
The people here taught their children to read the old letters out loud in the square.
Whoever lived here never threw away a good plank.
The people here kept a spare bed in every house for travellers.
The townsfolk here took turns ringing the bell, and everyone rang it differently.
conclusion: The Archive kept it whole. Somewhere a seed is waiting for a town like that.
Nothing here was lost. It was only waiting for someone to look.
It feels like visiting relatives you never met.
Your own town would get along with this one.
The network remembers. Now someone does too.
Somewhere, maybe, their great-grandchildren are building your neighbours' houses.
It is good to know a place like that existed.
The lantern of this town is a little brighter now, up at the Summit.
The memory goes back to sleep, gently, like a book being closed.
Leave it as you found it. That's what they would have done.
There's an idea here worth taking home.
Every town is different. Every town is a little bit the same.
It makes your own streets seem precious on the way back.
Somebody here would have liked you.
One more light on the old chart answers when called.
The Archive seems pleased that somebody came.
It's strange to be homesick for a town you never lived in.
Their song is quiet now, but it's still a song.
If you listen, you can hear their bell under yours.
The Mind of the Spire files it away again, a little less afraid.
There is no rush. The layer will still be here.
You climb on with their town in your pocket, like a pebble from a beach.
